title: It is I (John 6:16–21)
hookLine: rowing in the dark, they see him and he says: it is I, be not afraid
tomorrow: I am the bread of life

cards: Evening. Jesus is still alone up the mountain, and the disciples don't wait. They go down to the shore, get into the boat, and start rowing across the lake toward Capernaum.
"And it was now dark, and Jesus was not come to them." Then a great wind blows, and the sea rises. They row, and row.
And far out on the lake, in the dark, they see something on the water.

teach.b: "So when they had rowed about five and twenty or thirty furlongs, they see Jesus walking on the sea, and drawing nigh unto the ship: and they were afraid." And he says: "It is I; be not afraid."
In English, it is I sounds like any friend calling out in the dark: it's me. In Greek the words are ego eimi, which simply mean I am, the ordinary way to say it's me.
Some readers also hear in it the name God gives Moses at the burning bush, I AM.
John will use those two words again, and some readers hear both meanings here at once: it's me, your friend, and I AM, out on the water, where in the book of Job it is God who treads upon the waves.
Then the comfort: be not afraid. Fear not is said often in the Bible, by angels, by prophets, and by Jesus more than once.
John's ending is lovely and strange: "Then they willingly received him into the ship: and immediately the ship was at the land whither they went." No calming of the storm is described.

teach.h: HE GETS IN, AND THERE'S THE SHORE.
teach.b: Just him in the boat, and suddenly the shore.

teach.h: IT IS I; BE NOT AFRAID.
teach.b: This week: a water jar left at a well, a father walking home on a word, a man asked if he wanted to be well, God still working, the scriptures pointing, twelve baskets, and now a voice in the dark.

how: Some Christians turn to this story in times of fear, and "be not afraid" is repeated in prayers, in hymns and at bedsides.

games.q: you're rowing in the dark, miles from shore, and you see someone walking toward you on the water. what do you feel?
games.why: "they were afraid." then he speaks: "it is I; be not afraid," and they gladly take him into the boat.

practice: Close your eyes so it's a little dark, and let one fear you've been rowing against come up: money, health, someone you love, something you said.

Name it quietly in a few words, then imagine a voice you trust across the water: be not afraid. If you pray, invite Jesus into the boat with that fear; if you don't, let the words be a kindness to yourself.

wordCard.voice: Ego eimi. The Greek words behind it is I, meaning I am: what Jesus said to his friends in the dark, on the water.

orig.note: Greek: I am. The everyday way to say it's me, and to some readers an echo of the divine name in Exodus 3.
